source.title: Whisper Hallucination Detection and Mitigation via Hidden Representation Steering and Sparse AutoEncoders
source.authors: Georgii Aparin; Vadim Popov; Tasnima Sadekova; Assel Yermekova

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAEs and their sparse latent dimensions for hallucination detection and steering, motivated partly by superposition, but does not test the claim's feature-overlap geometry or its proposed explanations of polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The paper states that SAE classifier performance levels off when using roughly 50–100 top features and describes 10–25 dimensions as near-optimal. These findings concern how hallucination-related classification information is concentrated in SAE latents for Whisper, an audio ASR model, rather than testing the listed versions. The steering results measure the effectiveness and costs of the paper's own intervention; they do not test superposition or SAE feature properties named by the versions. The paper also discusses superposition as motivation and cites prior work, which is not evidence from this study.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained AudioSAE latents from Whisper, an ASR model and not an LLM, as a tool for hallucination classification and steering. It cites superposition only as motivation. It reports its own method's detection AUC and its steering trade-offs. It does not measure feature overlap, polysemanticity, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that hallucination information is linearly separable in Whisper activations and in SAE latents, and is concentrated in a few SAE dimensions. They conclude that SAE additive steering cuts hallucinations more than activation steering without fine-tuning (e.g. 72.63%→14.11% for small), approaching Calm-Whisper fine-tuned, with WER/CER trade-offs (Chinese CER degrades).
record.recipe_differences: The paper applies SAE classification and latent-space steering to Whisper ASR hallucinations; it does not reproduce the original toy-network method or measure overlapping feature directions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported top-k classification performance levels off around 50–100 features; the text also describes 10–25 dimensions as near-optimal.

fits_no_version.finding: For Whisper small and large-v3, hallucination-classification AUC from top-k SAE latents plateaus at about 50–100 features (Fig. 2). Steering works best with k=25 (small) and k=10 (large-v3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Whisper ASR encoders, hallucination-relevant information is concentrated in a small subset of SAE latents.

fits_no_version.finding: Passing activations through the SAE without steering (α=0) raises error rates. For large-v3, LibriSpeech-clean WER rises from 2.11 to 6.55. For small, CER on Chinese rises; the authors attribute this to the SAE being out of domain (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction in Whisper loses information needed for transcription, especially out of the SAE's training domain.

record.problems: The hallucination labels are assigned using Whisper's internal filtering rule rather than independently verified transcription ground truth. The top-k AUC values are presented in a figure without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Steering outcomes in Figures 3–5 and Tables 4–5 are omitted because they report the efficacy and ASR trade-offs of the paper's own method, not results testing the listed versions. Full-vector classification results in Table 3 are also omitted because they do not measure feature overlap, feature capacity, or the properties of SAE features named by the versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity sweep, no feature geometry.
Neuron polysemanticity and capacity competition are not measured.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity are not examined.
No LLMs are studied. Whether Whisper features are spread across neurons is not measured. SAE recovery of features is assumed, not evaluated.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. SAE reconstruction does degrade ASR quality, but this is not analysed as evidence on V5.
Dimensionality of features is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: This is an applied ASR paper. Superposition appears only as background motivation for SAEs. The SAE-reconstruction degradation could be of marginal interest to V5 reconstruction-fidelity work, but the study neither frames nor tests it that way.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-capacity sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or overlapping-direction geometry is tested.
No neuron polysemanticity or competition for limited representational capacity is measured.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons, or evidence against treating polysemanticity as evidence of superposition, are tested.
The study examines Whisper ASR rather than LLMs, and does not test whether LLM activations are distributed across neurons or whether SAE features recover their represented concepts.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
The study does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
